extracted.intended_audience: readers of Mark Twain / general literary readers and critics
extracted.subtask_description: A set of informal literary-evaluation criteria and letter-writing guidelines embedded in Mark Twain's letters (chiefly questions for assessing Sir Walter Scott's novels and some practical advice on complaint letters and views on originality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Address complaint to the head of the company
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring a complaint to the head of the company rather than to a subordinate for better effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘I bring it to you, the head of the company, because by experience I know better than to carry it to a subordinate.’ (Practical advice illustrated by Clemens' complaint about the telegraph service.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Precede complaints with a compliment
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a complaint, precede it with a compliment where possible to soften resentment and ensure a courteous reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘I think a compliment ought always to precede a complaint, where one is possible, because it softens resentment and insures for the complaint a courteous and gentle reception.’ (Applied in Clemens' Western Union letter.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using telegraph in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on the telegraph for urgent or emergency communications if alternatives exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clemens states he was 'afraid of the telegraph—which I think ought not to be used in times of hurry and emergency' and requested alternative delivery methods when urgency mattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and plagiarism principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Most intellectual output is second-hand; the substantive kernel of human utterance is largely plagiarism rather than absolute originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clemens argues: 'The kernel, the soul... of all human utterances, is plagiarism' and explains that originality is usually only a tiny 'discoloration' from an author's temperament; he gives examples (Dr. Holmes, dedications) and notes that exact reproduction of phrasing by adults is rare because memory is a palimpsest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passages done in good English
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there passages in the novel done in good English—English which is neither slovenly nor involved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 1 in Clemens' list to Brander Matthews; tests basic prose competence and clarity of expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passages of above-commonplace English
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there passages whose English is not poor and thin and commonplace, but is of a quality above that?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 2 in the list; distinguishes merely adequate prose from genuinely elevated or notable prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passages that 'burn with real fire'
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there passages which burn with real fire—not punk, fox-fire, make believe?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 3; looks for genuine passion or vigor in writing rather than fakery or superficial effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroes and heroines who are not cads and cadesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author provide heroes and heroines who are not morally compromised stock types (not cads and cadesses)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 4; evaluates the moral substance and worthiness of central characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts and speech matching character description
rubrics_metrics.description: Do personages' acts and talk correspond with their characters as described by the author?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 5; assesses internal consistency between characterization and behavior/dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elicits admiration with reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the author created heroes and heroines whom the reader admires and knows why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 6; distinguishes characters that merely appear admirable from those whose admirable qualities are convincingly shown and explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funny characters and genuinely humorous passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there funny characters that are funny, and humorous passages that are humorous?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 7; assesses quality and effectiveness of humor within the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to chain the reader's interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author 'chain the reader's interest' and make him reluctant to lay the book down?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 8; evaluates narrative propulsion, pacing, and the work's engrossing power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and absence of posing
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there pages where the author ceases from posing, ceases from admiring his own dilutions, ceases from being artificial, and is recognizably sincere and in earnest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 9; looks for moments of genuine artistic or emotional honesty amid possible affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's command of English vs. choice not to use it
rubrics_metrics.description: Did the author know how to write English, and didn't do it because he didn't want to?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 10; distinguishes between lack of skill and deliberate stylistic choices that may undercut quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision in word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the author use the right word only when he couldn't think of another one, or does he so often use the wrong word because he didn't know the right one when he saw it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 11; evaluates vocabulary precision and the author's ability to select apt diction rather than approximate or incorrect words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability combined with enduring respect
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you read him and keep your respect for him?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question 13; a holistic test combining immediate readability with lasting esteem for the author and his work.
